rejected.title: Judging statistics in the media
card: A news report may quote a study. Before you trust it, ask who was asked and how they were chosen.
Ask how many people were in the study. A very small sample gives a less reliable result than a large one.
Ask who paid for the study. A group that gains from a result may have a reason to present it in its favour.
Ask whether the claim goes further than the data. A link between two things does not prove one causes the other, and a result about one group may not hold for everyone.
rejected.remember: Check who was asked, how many, who paid, and whether the claim fits the data.

a.q: A headline says 'Most Australians love our juice'. It is based on 12 customers at one shop. Which check does this fail most clearly?
opts: The sample is small and from one place
The study was paid for by a government
The sample was chosen at random
The data was collected over a week
a.why: Twelve customers at one shop is a very small group and cannot stand for most Australians. The claim goes further than the data. Random choice would be a strength, not a problem.
a.clue: Count the people, then think about where they came from.

b.q: A company that makes Stride shoes pays for a survey of 2000 adults. People in it who wear Stride shoes run faster on average. Which conclusion does this data support?
opts: Stride wearers in the survey ran faster on average
Wearing Stride shoes makes people run faster
Anyone who buys Stride shoes will run faster
Fast runners are more likely to choose Stride shoes
b.why: The survey shows only a link among the people asked. Other things, such as fitness, could explain it, so the data cannot prove the shoes make anyone faster. The tempting option says the shoes cause faster running, which claims more than the data shows.
b.clue: Does a link between two things prove one causes the other?

b.q: A shoe company pays for a survey of 2000 randomly chosen adults. It reports that people who wear its shoes run faster, so its shoes make you faster. What is the best criticism?
opts: The data may not show the shoes cause faster running
The sample of 2000 adults is far too small
The adults were not chosen at random
The survey was too large to give any result
b.why: The data may show only a link. Other things, such as fitness, could explain faster running, so the claim goes further than the data. The sample is fairly large and random, so those are not the main problem.
b.clue: Does a link between two things prove one causes the other?

a.best: The sample is small and from one place

b.best: The data may not show the shoes cause faster running

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a hedge ('may not show'). Two distractors contradict the stem outright: it says the adults were randomly chosen, and calling 2000 'far too small' or 'too large' is clearly wrong. A student can rule these out without understanding cause versus link.
